title: Depart content
hook: Marcus ends: go gladly, for the one who dismisses you is gracious (Meditations 12.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a small share of time, given, not earned. Your line was a small share. What did you spend yours on that you'd spend it on again? Day six hundred thirty-six.

The last line of a book carries weight. Readers remember it. Writers sweat over it. Marcus Aurelius almost certainly never meant his notebook to be a book at all, so we can't be sure he chose his last line. But the passage that stands at the end, as the book has come down to us, is about a stage, an actor, and a man in charge of the show who says: that's enough, you can go. It's about death, and it's surprisingly gentle. Today: the last words of the Meditations.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF A BOOK.` → `AN ACTOR, A STAGE, "THAT'S ENOUGH."` → `THE LAST WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. In 12.36 Marcus pictures a comic actor whom the official in charge of the games dismisses from the stage. The actor protests: but I've only played three of the five acts. And the answer comes back, in effect: in life, three acts can be the whole play. The one who put the drama together decides when it's complete, and the one who ends it does too. You were the cause of neither. Second, the line itself, in George Long's translation: "Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied." The Greek word Long renders satisfied is hileōs, which also means gracious, kindly, at peace. So you could hear it both ways: go at peace, because the one releasing you is at peace with you. Go gladly, because you're being dismissed kindly, not thrown out. Third, who that one is. Marcus doesn't say. Stoics spoke of nature, of the whole, of God or the gods, and he uses all of those words in the book. Some readers hear a personal God. Some hear nature itself, the order that brought you onto the stage. The text leaves room for both. Fourth, why it's for the living. You don't have to be dying to use this. Every day ends before you've finished everything. Every job, every season, every conversation gets called before act five. Marcus's last word is practice for the small endings: leave the stage without clutching the curtain.
screen: `THE ACTOR WITH THREE ACTS DONE.` · `HILEŌS: SATISFIED, GRACIOUS.` · `WHO RELEASES YOU? HE DOESN'T SAY.` · `PRACTICE FOR SMALL ENDINGS.` · then, large: `GO GLADLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Think of today as a play with acts. Name the ones already done: the morning, the work, whatever came. Some went well, some didn't. Notice anything you're still clutching, a task half-done, a conversation you'd like a rewrite of. Now picture the curtain for today, a few hours from now. If you can, let today be complete as it is, three acts or five. Say to yourself, in your own words, that it was enough. The bell holds the time.
Depart content. The last words of the Meditations: leave the stage at peace, because the one who releases you is at peace too. Today's word.
Your line: go gladly. Tonight, when you close the laptop or turn off the light, end the day on purpose, as a finished play, not an interrupted one. Day six hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Readers often treat the last passage of the Meditations as an evening practice, ending the day as a complete act rather than an unfinished one.

fork.setup: you're the actor, pulled off the stage after act three. what does the last passage of the Meditations invite you to do?
options: argue for your last two acts.
go at peace, since the one who releases you is at peace.
fork.reveal: Marcus ends with the actor going satisfied, because the one who dismisses him is gracious. it's practice for every small ending, too.

original.note: Greek: gracious, kindly, at peace. Used twice in the last sentence of the Meditations: go hileōs, for the one who releases you is hileōs.

trapdoor: what you thought: depart content is a grim line about dying.
what it means: go at peace when your time on the stage is called, because you're being released kindly.

what a scholar hears: the actor-and-play image is a Stoic commonplace (Epictetus uses it too), and hileōs echoes language used of gods who are gracious, which lets the line be heard religiously or naturally.
